hook.text: The Romans built aqueducts to carry water 60 miles — gravity alone did the work.

buildup.text: Canals are artificial open channels. They carry irrigation water, drinking water, or ships.

discovery.text: Lined canals use concrete to prevent seepage. Unlined canals lose 30-50% to the ground.

twist.text: The California Aqueduct carries Sierra Nevada snowmelt 444 miles south to Los Angeles.

climax.text: Modern canals include automated gates that adjust flow in real time using sensors.

punchline.text: Move water by gravity across hundreds of miles. The Romans did it. We still do.

quiz.question: Why are many modern canals lined with concrete?
options: To make the canal look more attractive
To prevent water from seeping into the ground and being lost
To increase the speed of boat traffic in the canal

details.summary: Canals and aqueducts transport water over long distances for irrigation, water supply, navigation, and hydropower. Gravity-fed systems follow gentle gradients across terrain using tunnels, siphons, and elevated structures to maintain continuous flow.
details.whyItMatters: Large-scale water conveyance enables civilization in arid regions by transporting water from wet areas to dry ones. California's State Water Project and China's South-North Transfer demonstrate the scale of modern water conveyance systems.
takeaways: Gravity canals follow gentle slopes of 0.01-0.1% to move water without pumping energy
Inverted siphons carry canal flows under valleys and obstructions using pressure pipe
Concrete lining prevents seepage losses that can waste 30-50% of flow in unlined canals

faq.question: How do engineers move canal water across valleys and ridges?
faq.answer: Valleys are crossed using inverted siphons where the canal drops into a pressure pipe, crosses the valley floor, and rises to the canal on the opposite side. Ridges require either tunnels bored through the obstacle or pumping stations that lift water over the high point.

faq.question: Why do canals lose so much water to seepage?
faq.answer: Unlined earth canals allow water to infiltrate through the bed and banks into surrounding soil, losing 30-50% of flow over long distances. Concrete or geomembrane lining reduces losses to under 5%.
